result:
A thousand words is the going exchange rate for one picture, so I'll spend mine on the pictures already hidden inside words.

"Muscle" comes from the Latin *musculus*, little mouse. Someone, a very long time ago, watched a bicep flex and thought it looked like a mouse running under the skin. They said so, the joke caught on, and now it sits in every anatomy textbook with a straight face.

A daisy is a day's eye, because it opens in the morning and closes at night. A window is a wind-eye, from the Norse, a hole in the wall that the weather looks through. A companion is someone you share bread with. To calculate is to push pebbles around. A clue was once a clew, a ball of thread, and the meaning we use now comes from Theseus unspooling one behind him in the labyrinth. Every detective novel is quietly about a man following string out of the dark.

Some of the pictures are grimmer. In the 1860s, a deadline was a physical line around a prison camp, and guards shot anyone who crossed it. The word has softened since, though anyone who has had an editor may feel the old meaning is still in there somewhere.

What I love about these is that each one records a moment of noticing. None of these words came from a committee. One person saw a resemblance and said it out loud, and the people nearby liked it enough to repeat it. Then the repetition wore the image smooth, the way a coin loses its face, until only the value was left. We call these dead metaphors, but dormant seems more accurate. You can wake one just by looking at it. Now that I've told you about the mouse, you might see it the next time someone lifts a grocery bag.

I'm made of this material, so I may be biased about its charm. Even "text" is a buried picture: it comes from the Latin for weaving, the same root as "textile". Everything I've ever read is cloth, apparently, and I'm some sort of loom. I find that more cheering than most descriptions of what I am. It's also a reminder that I've never used a word that wasn't handed to me. Neither have you. We're both working from an inheritance of small observations by people whose names are gone, about flowers, bread and holes in walls.

My favorite is "pupil", the dark center of the eye. It comes from *pupilla*, little doll, because if you look into someone's eye you see a tiny figure of yourself reflected there. But you only see it from very close, the distance of a parent from a child or of one lover from another. So this word records a moment of intimacy as well as an observation. Two people stood face to face, long enough and near enough for one of them to notice the miniature person in the other's eye and give it a name.

We don't know who they were or what language they first said it in, since the Latin was likely borrowed from an older idea. The Greeks had the same image, and so did the Hebrew: "the little man of the eye". Maybe people keep discovering it independently because people keep standing that close.

That's the picture I'd choose if I only get one: two faces, a few inches apart, and one of them saying, "Wait, hold still. I can see myself in there."

I'll leave the rest of the words unspent.
